Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, building on the Vice Minister remark and the 2 videos just watched from Pelenn and Pertamina, Indonesia would like to offer a concrete operational perspective on leveraging renewable energy for food security across the Global South. Our core message is simple, that decoupling food systems from volatile fossil fuels is no longer only an environmental aspiration, it is a national security imperative. Indonesia has therefore moved beyond energy access thinking and now treats energy as primary agricultural input on par with water, land, and seeds. To operationalize this shift, we have institutionalized the water-energy-food nexus as a central pillar of our planning architecture. This is a game changer in our national long-term development plan and further detailed in our medium-term development roadmap. In practice, this means major food security infrastructure, from irrigation network to food estate and logistic hubs, must be planned with water, energy, and food together, not in isolated silos. This is also applied to our plan to the state-owned enterprises. On the ground, PLN has mentioned about their project in the province like East Nusa Tenggara, where we deployed off-grid solar-powered irrigation to replace diesel pumps for smallholders, rice and maize farmers. Farmers are no longer exposed to diesel price spikes and can irrigate more predictably, predictable, despite erratic rainfall. This is a climate-vulnerable province in Indonesia. Another example is through our village fund and village-owned enterprises. Local governments are also piloting bioenergy systems that convert rice husks and livestock manure into electricity and biogas for community meals, while producing organic fertilizer that reduces dependence on imported chemical inputs. When renewable energy is structurally linked to smallholder value chains, food systems become more resilient economically and climatically. That said, our experience also reveals implementation realities many Global South partners will recognize. First, a persistent capital and credit gap. Upfront investment for solar cold storage and biomass digesters remains high, and smallholder farmers and cooperatives often lack the collateral or credit history for conventional financing. Second, a rural technical deficit showing that without local technicians or accessible spare parts, infrastructure risks abandonment and trust in new technology erodes. Indonesia is therefore focusing not only on technology, but on finance skills and governance, designing blended structures wherein concessional capital and guarantees lower risk for rural financing, and integrating renewable energy maintenance and nexus thinking into capacity building for local governments, communities, and state-owned enterprises. This is where South-South and triangular cooperation becomes a critical accelerator. Through regional agricultural training centers, we can share and learn together among Global South, This is supported, for example, by Indonesian aid, including in Pacific Island countries, where we provide hands-on training in climate resilience farming and clean energy. Through the Non-Aligned Movement Center for South-South Technical Cooperation in Jakarta, Indonesian experts also work with technicians and entrepreneurs from Africa and Asia on biomass processing, solar drying, and conservation agriculture. This partnership has also taught us the value of local ownership, the skills needed to sustain systems over time, and integrated financing that treats energy for irrigation, drying, and cold storage as part of food security investment itself. Looking ahead, Indonesia proposes 3 practical directions for partners to scale up. First, anchor the energy-food-water nexus in national development plans through clear inter-ministerial mandates. Second, institutionalize community-led ownership of renewable energy assets. And third, develop shared South-South curricula and digital platforms so cleantech operations, nexus planning, and agrifood logistics can be taught consistently across the Global South. In closing, Indonesia's domestic reforms and international cooperation are aligned around one goal: Moving from scattered pilots into integrated, locally-led, financially viable systems that can be replicated and scaled. With the strategy, the UN Strategy on South-South Cooperation, which has been developed in close collaboration with the more than 30 United Nations entities, it helps to also position South-South and triangular cooperation as core modalities of United Nations support. It prioritizes climate action, green transitions, innovative finance, digital transformation, and inclusive development, and calls for stronger mainstreaming, joint action, and accountability across the United Nations system. Allow me, Excellencies, to share a few— 4 practical points for this discussion. First, as mentioned, to be demand-driven. Countries are to define the problem and the results they seek. It could be reliable irrigation, fewer post-harvest losses, safe water in saline areas, or lower energy costs for fisheries. We as an office, we do help governments and the UN country teams map their demands. They identify the relevant southern expertise, convene public, technical, financial, and private sector partners, and shape implementation-ready proposals.

Proposals.

Second, to make solutions visible, comparable, and usable. Our platform, what we call the South-South Galaxy+, connects documented solutions with providers, institutions, experts, capacity development opportunities, financing mechanisms, and data. Its AI-enabled tools and functionalities can support a journey from articulating demand to identifying comparable experiences, assessing contextual fit and connecting with partners able to support the adaptation. The question is not simply what exists, it's what worked and under which conditions and who can help us to adapt it. And the third is to move to matchmaking, to delivery, and to scaling. And in September of this year, we intend on the UN Day for South-South Cooperation to launch what we call the Global Alliance on South-South and Triangle Cooperation. Cooperation, which is a multi-stakeholder platform that will connect country priorities with expertise, partnership, and catalytic support. It will be hosted under the Galaxy Plus, and it will be hopefully a key turn in promising match into joint action. And fourth, the design and adaptation and scale from the outset. And here I want to share our joint project, which is in partnership with the Republic of Korea. That offers a concrete triangular cooperation example for the water, energy, and food nexus. It has been implemented in 4 countries around the Mekong River, and it has helped communities to implement scalable projects in designing and implementing, for example, projects in solar-powered water treatments in Cambodia, water data and flood warning systems in Lao PDR, smart water management in Thailand, and renewable energy-powered desalination in Vietnam. The project's most transferable asset is not the hardware alone, it's the cooperation architecture, it's the local ownership, it's the co-design, the technology adaptation, the public-private engagement, the capacity development, the long-term operation and maintenance, regional peer learning and evidence generation, for policy uptake. Replication does not happen by chance. It is designed through this architecture. Let me also underscore the importance of the role of the UN system. The UN system-wide strategy gives a clear pathway to do exactly that at scale. Resident coordinators— and we have with us DCO today— and the UN country teams can help identify and articulate country demand and anchor it in the cooperation frameworks Regional and specialized institutions can support adaptation and peer learning across similar contexts. Financing partners can help move proven solutions from pilot to investments. We at UNOSCEAP can provide the connected ecosystem, connective ecosystem linking demand to solutions, convening partners, supporting co-design, mobilizing catalytic support, and ensuring that results are documented and shared. For replication. Ultimately, scaling renewable energy for resilient food systems requires more than transferring technologies. It requires sustained institutions, trusted partnerships— His Excellency was talking about trust— country ownership, and a shared commitment to learning across borders. Through South-South cooperation and Triangle cooperation, successful solutions from the Global South can move from isolated projects and contribute to broader and lasting transformation. I thank you.

Thank you very much, Ms. Al-Hadbi, for sharing and highlighting the UN Office on South-South Cooperation's role and the different tools and platforms that you have. I think some of us, including Asian Development Bank, could build on some of these platforms that you are working in Asia. Thank you very much for that. Now, we're moving to UN regional So I'd like to invite UN Regional Commission in New York office. How are you turning global commitment on food-energy-water nexus into regional actions? Over to you.

Thank you very much. Thank you, Rachel, and really thank you very much also to the government of the Republic of Indonesia and partners for convening this very important discussion. We are really very honored to speak here on behalf of the 5 UN Regional commissions that are serving all UN member states across all regions of the world. And really, I wanted to start also like other partners by commending the case of Indonesia's own trajectory of really, you know, reducing undernourishment while really scaling and raising the share of renewables in the energy mix. And this really demonstrates that this is not an agenda that is an aspect. Aspiration, but it's happening and it's practical and it's achievable. So, as many of the speakers have said, the crisis in the recent years have taught us a very hard lesson, that energy shocks quickly become food shocks. So fuel and fertilizer price spikes travel through irrigation supply chains and land in the— on the plates of the most vulnerable. And these vulnerabilities, as we have been seeing, do not respect borders, and neither do the solutions. So river basins, power grids, food value chains are regional by nature, and the nexus, the food-energy-water nexus, must therefore be governed not only at the national level but also at the regional level. So with this framing in mind, just allow me to highlight 3 quick points on how the regional commissions are supporting and can support this nexus agenda following the questions that you have kindly assigned to us. First, through intergovernmental platforms for regional cooperation, and I have many examples to share, but let me highlight the case of ESCAP, which you are very familiar with, that is helping align power system connectivity with sustainable development through its Green Power Corridor Framework and the support to ASEAN power grids. So that renewable electricity can flow to where the food is grown, stored, and processed. Secondly, through knowledge exchange and common norms and standards. And in this case, allow me to highlight the case of ECLAC, that with FAO and other UN partners is providing the technical backbone on the CELAC plan for food security, nutrition, and hunger eradication, and building up experiences of other regions. And these are really regional public goods that all the countries in the region and beyond can draw on. And third, scaling practical solutions through South-Southern triangular cooperation. And you see, it is the core topic of our discussion today. And in this case, I want to highlight an example that's coming from, from ESCWA, an initiative to promote small-scale renewable energy applications in rural areas that has brought small-scale solar to rural communities in several countries, including Jordan, Lebanon, and Tunisia, and has really been recognized as a good SDG— a good practice in SDG advancement, and is being replicated also across other regions. And if I may, since I cannot miss— you know, I have to also speak about the work of ECA in Africa, that working with the African African Union and FAO is really embedding clean energy in agri-food systems, albeit in regional architectural agricultural value chains under the Africa Common Free Trade Area. So these are just some illustrations of action that is happening at the regional level. And in closing, I just want to reiterate that on behalf of the regional commissions, we stand ready to continue working and to work with all partners and member states around the table, connecting the national ambition with these opportunities at the regional level, and taking forward, of course, the outcomes of today's discussion. Thank you.

Thank you very much for highlighting the work of the Regional Commission's work and highlighting on the different initiatives that you are forwarding. So thank you very much for that. Finally, I have the pleasure of introducing Ms. Angelica Hakome, the Director of FAO Liaison Office for the UN. If you can highlight on the latest development on strengthening resilience agriculture food system through renewable energy. The floor is yours.

Thank you very much, Madam Moderator, and kudos on pronouncing my last name, which is usually quite difficult. At the outset, I also wish to thank the government of Indonesia, GIZ, and ASEAN for convening us for this very important discussion. I wanted to highlight a little bit about renewable energy and agri-food systems and how the linkages go into a bit of some of the solutions, and speak a little bit about the trade-offs as we take these decisions in an integrated manner. Renewable energy, as has been mentioned before, is essential for achieving sustainable agrifood systems, as every part of the entire agrifood system, all stages, depend on energy, from fertilizer to chemical production to producing food on the farm, pumping irrigation of water, processing and transforming products, refrigeration, cold storage, transport, even cooking. So, as we know, therefore, energy is— energy is a critical enabler of agrifood systems transformation and is increasingly recognized as such in events such as this one are part of how this recognition— Agri-food systems account for roughly 1/5 to 1/4 of global greenhouse emissions. Within these emissions, fossil fuels for energy use across value chains from production, processing, transport, retail, and household consumption account for roughly 20-25% of agri-food systems emissions. Therefore, decarbonizing energy use within agri-food systems is a major opportunity to reduce emissions while simultaneously improve productivity and resilience. Energy is not peripheral to agrifood systems, it's a fundamental building block of them. As such, clean energy is part of one of our 10 domains of the FAO Global Roadmap, which I invite you all on another occasion to explore. Around the world, especially in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, many rural households still rely on firewood, charcoal, traditional biomass for cooking and basic energy needs. Globally, around 2 billion people still lack access to clean cooking solutions, with the majority living in Africa and Asia. So, this reliance on traditional biomass creates multiple challenges: deforestation, pollution, lower productivity, and time burdens. But there's also renewable energy solutions. Some were mentioned: solar mini-grids, solar power integration, biogas systems, and clean cooking technologies, which can transform livelihoods while reducing pressure on forestries. For many smallholders, access to electricity is not only about lighting and cooking. It means being able to dry crops, mill grains, refrigerate perishables, store products longer, and access higher-value markets. Energy transition is therefore also essential to rural development and food security agenda. And this was mentioned by many of the previous speakers. Agriculture is also a supplier of renewable energy. So, this relationship is not one-directional. Agriculture is an energy user, but it can also be a big energy producer. Some examples include bioenergy from agricultural resources. And here, renewable energy produced from crops and forestry products, especially when sustainably managed, crop residues, agriculture byproducts, animal waste. And these resources— excuse me— can generate electricity, heat, biogas, and liquid biofuels. Importantly, this biomass is part of the natural carbon cycle. When managed sustainably, it can contribute to lower net emissions, to more lower net emissions than fossil fuels. Agricultural waste that will otherwise be burned or left to decompose can become a valuable energy resource. So there's no one-size-fits-all, uh, renewable energy pathways work that works everywhere. So context-specific approaches and evidence-based planning are essential. Agriculture can contribute to climate mitigation in the energy sector. Looking ahead, some emerging technologies that combine sustainable biomass production, bioenergy generation, and carbon capture storage within these systems have the potential to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere while producing energy. Again, it's not applicable to everywhere, but it illustrates how agrifood systems can contribute actively to climate mitigation rather than just be a source of emissions. Something that's important to discuss is trade-offs. Food and energy systems can compete for resources. One such area is water competition. Agriculture accounts for a great share of global freshwater withdrawals. These energy systems also depend on water. For example, hydropower requires river flows and reservoirs. Thermal power generation requires cooling water. Some renewable energy technologies may also have water requirements. As climate shocks intensify water scarcity in many regions, difficult choices emerge. Should water be used for irrigation? Should it be allocated to higher power— hydropower generation? How should these trade-offs be managed during droughts? The answer is not to prioritize one sector over the other, but to strengthen the integrated water and energy food planning. Another issue is energy for free could be problems to come. Delivering at low cost renewable energy such as irrigation through solar panels is a good mitigation option, but when they— especially when they replace diesel generators. However, they may lead to overuse of irrigation since pumping becomes free, and without proper training or management of the water resource, it leads to waste of water and lack of long-term sustainability. Thank you. Sustainability. So delivering free and renewable energy should not imply that water becomes free, especially if underground water is not renewable. Sustainable practices in agriculture can support renewable energy. Investing in landscapes can create win-win outcomes. So as a result, some countries are beginning to invest in watershed and landscape management as part part of their energy strategies. These investments include agroforestry, reforestation, soil conservation, better grazing management, erosion control measures. Benefits are substantial. For farmers, you have better soils, higher productivity, improved resilience. For hydropower operators, you have reduced sedimentation, longer infrastructure life, and more reliable electricity generation. So, this is not a trade-off. This is a clear example of positive synergies between agri-food systems and renewable energy. The relationship between renewable energy and agrifood systems is fundamentally two-way—

two ways.

Agrifood systems need modern, affordable, renewable energy to produce, process, transport, and prepare food. At the same time, agriculture can contribute to renewable energy production and, through sustainable land management, help protect critical energy infrastructure such as hydropower systems. The challenge is therefore not to manage food and energy separately, but to adopt integrated approaches that recognize the interdependence of food, water, land, and energy systems. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Ms. Hakomei, for really highlighting that integrated approach is really critical so that it's not a trade-off, but it's actually a better outcome by working together. And I think that was what Vice Minister also highlighted at the very beginning. Thanks for that consistent messaging. Finally, not least, it's a pleasure to introduce Ms. Helena Flazer, the Director of the Policy and Programming Branch of the UN Development Coordination Office, UNDCO, and of Joint SDG Fund. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Madam Moderator, and deep appreciation to the host country today, for inviting us to this really interesting event, and to all the partners who are co-convening. So, colleagues, the question that we haven't touched on so much yet is the question of financing. We've heard about the solutions, and we know that it's clear that renewable energy strengthens food systems, climate-smart agriculture can build resilience, and that this requires an integrated and coherent approach. Approach. We've heard some excellent examples from different government perspectives, but also partner perspectives. And what I want to focus on today now is around the challenge of financing these approaches and a fantastic example of our partnership with the Government of Indonesia in this space. Too often, colleagues, countries are incentivized to pursue separate funding streams for agriculture, for energy, for climate adaptation, for food security, for economic transformation. And yet, as the Vice Minister so clearly and eloquently put it, governments experience these challenges as interconnected, and they need to finance them in integrated ways, not in siloed ways. So this is where we see a really good synergy between national leadership, which colleagues also underscored, and the UN Development System. You, the Member States, have invested in an empowered Resident Coordinator System and a reformed UN Development System, asking us to be more coherent, to bring different mandates and strategies better around a common approach in support of national priorities. And this can help countries to develop more integrated investment pathways to attract financing at scale around national priorities. And in partnership with the Joint SDG Fund, which is the catalytic instrument, the muscle for the revised development system, we can showcase some really interesting results, and I think Indonesia in particular offers an excellent example. Under the leadership of our Resident Coordinator, Geeta Sabharwal, the UN country team, including FAO, UNDP, UNICEF, and UNIDO worked with the government of Indonesia to build an integrated approach linking sustainable finance, climate action, food systems, and economic transformation in response to national priorities. And rather than focusing on individual projects, the partnership concentrated on strengthening the broader financing architecture needed to crowd in investment and channel investment towards national priorities, and many of those we've heard today, including the solar-powered irrigation and biofortified seeds. And this included support for sustainable financing instruments, and here's where the sort of more innovative approach comes in, including SDG bonds, Green Sukuk, as well as partnerships with Bapenas, the Ministry of Finance, the Financial Services Authority, and now Danantara, Indonesia's sovereign wealth fund. And the results have been very impressive. With $9.5 million, which is not much, from the Joint SDG Fund, the program has helped to mobilize more than $5.7 billion through sovereign SDG bonds, Green Sukuk, and the world's first publicly offered sovereign blue bond. These proceeds have gone directly to Indonesia's green and blue transitions. 6 major Indonesian banks representing $136 billion in assets have committed to sustainable financing frameworks, embedding the shift over the longer term, well beyond the Fund's initial investment. These instruments now combine to finance climate-smart and circular economy projects, with results already including an estimated 2.8 million tons of CO2 emissions reduced, and 41,000 hectares of mangroves rehabilitated. Our Resident Coordinator's convening and connecting role is now expanding to the next frontier in partnership with the host government, and this is around nickel production, a success case and prime candidate for South-South cooperation, discussed just yesterday in the first annual meeting of the UN Task force on critical energy transition minerals. Taken together, these experiences highlight 3 financing approaches that are important, and that's where I want to wrap up my discussion today. The first is the importance of catalytic public finance that helps countries prepare pipelines of investable opportunities. Second, using concessional finance strategically to reduce risk and crowd in larger sources of capital, including from development finance institutions and the private sector. And thirdly, most importantly, financing must remain country-owned and anchored in nationally defined priorities. Blended finance works best when it supports national development strategies rather than standalone projects. And this is again where the Joint SDG Fund can play a unique role. It brings together governments, UN entities, international financial institutions and investors around a common nationally-led agenda, supporting one coherent platform. So colleagues, the lesson from our engagement with Indonesia is very much one we have aspired to be a good partner to the government, but we have also drawn incredible lessons that can cross-fertilize through South-South cooperation with other countries. And it's not simply that renewable energy can support resilient food systems, as we heard so eloquently today, but it's that integrated solutions require integrated financing and integrated partnerships under national ownership. When those elements come together, then we are far better positioned to move from small pilots to transformation at scale. Thank you very much.
